title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 389
paragraphs: It is said, however, that even when he was a commoner, Amasis was a lover of drinking and jesting, and not at all seriously disposed. Whenever his means of livelihood failed him through his drinking and luxurious living, he would go about and steal; and those he stole from would accuse him of having their property, and when he denied it, they would bring him before the judgment of an oracle whenever there was one in the place. Many times he was convicted by the oracles, and many times he was acquitted. When he finally became king, he did as follows: as for all those gods who had acquitted him and pronounced him not to be a thief, he paid no regard to their temples, gave nothing for their further adornment, and did not even visit them to offer sacrifice, considering them worthless and their oracles lying; but as for those who had convicted him of being a thief, to these he paid the very greatest regard, considering them to be true gods and to give oracles that did not lie.
